summary: This document reserves ranges of numbers for experimenting in specific protocols, namely IPv4, IPv6, ICMPv4, ICMPv6, UDP and TCP headers, where the need was identified. It also describes numbers already reserved for this by other documents, so experiments need not use real assigned values.

plainLanguage.summary: To test a new protocol you need a number for it, such as a port or a field value in a packet header. This RFC lists the numbers that are set aside for that purpose, so an experiment does not have to borrow a number that something else already uses.

questions: which ip protocol numbers are for experiments
subtitle: Reserved numbers for testing new protocols without taking a real value.

tldr.problem: Testing a new protocol needs a protocol number, a port or an option value, but picking a real assigned value risks interfering with services that are already running.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records the values reserved for experiments in the IPv4 and IPv6 headers, in ICMP, in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and in the UDP and TCP headers, following the guidance in RFC 3692.
tldr.outcome: Each reserved value is meant for explicitly configured experiments and must not be shipped as a default in an implementation, so production networks may still drop traffic that uses them.

today: RFC 4727 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the experimental values it reserves; the general guidance for such values is in RFC 3692.

sections.title: Why Experiments Need Reserved Numbers
sections.content:
Testing or extending a protocol usually requires a protocol number or a constant, even when the test happens in a closed environment. The values come from registries that IANA administers, and RFC 3692 sets out how numbers should be assigned for experiments and testing. This document lists the assignments that were needed for particular header fields, and follows the form of RFC 2780.

Using one of these values takes care. The advice in Sections 1 and 1.1 of RFC 3692 applies: it is not appropriate to simply select one of the values and hard code it into a system.

RFC 3692 also says it may not be necessary to allocate values for UDP and TCP ports, but this document reserves two anyway, in Sections 6 and 7.1, to remove any chance of a conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol field has a registry of numbers that decide what each value means. This RFC lists the entries in those registries that are kept for experiments, so a test does not collide with a real service.

sections.title: Protocol Numbers in the IP Headers
sections.content:
The IPv4 header has fields whose values are assigned by IANA: Version, Type of Service, Protocol, Source Address, Destination Address and Option Type. The IPv6 header has its own set: Version, Traffic Class, Next Header, Source and Destination Address, plus Option Type fields in the Hop-by-Hop and Destination Options extension headers.

Some fields need no new entries. The IPv4 Version field is always 4 and the IPv6 Version field is always 6. RFC 2474 already defines Pool 2, all code points of the form xxxx11, as Experimental or Local Use, so the Type of Service and Traffic Class fields need no extra code points, and the Explicit Congestion Notification field has no free code points to assign at all.

Two code points, 253 and 254, are available for experiments in the IPv4 Protocol field, and the same two values are available in the IPv6 Next Header field. They come from the experimental allocations made by RFC 3692.
sections.plainLanguage: The Protocol field in IPv4 and the Next Header field in IPv6 say which protocol a packet carries. The values 253 and 254 are kept aside so a test can use them without colliding with a real protocol.

sections.title: Experimental Addresses and Multicast Groups
sections.content:
For IPv4 unicast addresses, no experimental addresses are defined. The address ranges set aside for private internets by RFC 1918 may be useful for some experiments, but the other special-purpose IPv4 addresses listed in RFC 3330 are not appropriate. Some registries have policies that allow experimental assignments from the number spaces they control, which may be a path to pursue depending on the experiment.

For IPv4 multicast, the globally routable group 224.0.1.20 is set aside for experimentation, and the administratively scoped multicast groups of RFC 2365 may also be useful. This document assigns a single link-local scoped group, 224.0.0.254, and a single scope-relative group, 254.

For IPv6 unicast, no RFC 3692 style experimental addresses are assigned at the time of writing, although RFC 2928 sets aside the block of Sub-TLA IDs assigned to IANA, from 2001:0000::/29 to 2001:01F8::/29, for testing and experimental usage. Unique Local Addresses from RFC 4193 may be useful, but the documentation prefix of RFC 3849 is not appropriate. For IPv6 multicast, the group FF0X::114 is set aside for experimentation at all scope levels, and multicast addresses with the transient bit set may be useful.
sections.plainLanguage: An experiment also needs addresses to send to. The RFC points at the address ranges and multicast groups that are safe to use, and names the ones that are not meant for experiments.

sections.title: Experimental Options in IPv4 and IPv6
sections.content:
The IPv4 Option Type field is assigned a single option number with all defined values of its copy and class fields, which results in four distinct option type codes: 30, 94, 158 and 222.

The IPv6 Hop-by-Hop and Destination Option fields are assigned a single option type with all possible values of the act and chg fields, which results in eight distinct option type codes: 0x1e, 0x3e, 0x5e, 0x7e, 0x9e, 0xbe, 0xde and 0xfe.

The IPv6 Routing Header has a Type field for which there is no explicit IANA assignment policy, so this document assigns two values to it, 253 and 254.
sections.plainLanguage: Options are extra fields that can be added to a packet header. This RFC sets aside a handful of option codes in IPv4, IPv6 and the IPv6 routing header so an experiment can carry an option nobody else uses.

sections.title: ICMP, Neighbor Discovery and Port Numbers
sections.content:
This document assigns two ICMPv4 type numbers, 253 and 254. ICMPv4 code values are allocated per type, so it is not feasible to assign experimental values for them here.

For ICMPv6, RFC 4443 already includes experimental type values for Informational messages, 200 and 201, and for Error messages, 100 and 101. ICMPv6 code values are also allocated per type. In IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, the Type field is the same as the ICMPv6 Type field, the Code field is not used, and two Option Types, 253 and 254, are assigned.

Two system ports, 1021 and 1022, are reserved for experimentation for UDP and TCP. The TCP header has too few reserved bits to allocate any for experiments, but two TCP options, 253 and 254, are reserved for experimentation with TCP options.
sections.plainLanguage: The same pattern applies to the control messages and to the transport protocols. Two ICMPv4 types, two Neighbor Discovery options, two TCP options and the ports 1021 and 1022 are kept aside for tests.

sections.title: The Registered Values
sections.content:
The new assignments are summarized in the registry tables. The IPv4 multicast registry receives 224.0.0.254 in the Local Network Control Block section and the relative address 254. The IPv4 option number registry receives 30, 94, 158 and 222. The IPv6 option type registry receives 0x1e, 0x3e, 0x5e, 0x7e, 0x9e, 0xbe, 0xde and 0xfe, and the IPv6 Routing Header type registry receives 253 and 254. The ICMPv4 type registry receives 253 and 254, the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option registry receives 253 and 254, the TCP option registry receives 253 and 254, and the system port registry receives the keywords exp1 and exp2 for 1021 and 1022 over both UDP and TCP.

Every one of these registrations carries the same footnote: it is only appropriate to use these values in explicitly configured experiments, and they MUST NOT be shipped as defaults in implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists each reserved value in the registry it belongs to. Every entry carries a warning that the value is for configured experiments only and must never be the default in a product.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Production networks do not necessarily support experimental code points in IP headers. The reach of that support should be evaluated before an experiment is deployed across extended network domains such as the public Internet, because disrupting the stable operation of the network is a serious consideration when planning an experiment.

Security analyzers such as firewalls and intrusion detection monitors rely on unambiguous interpretations of these fields. An analyzer that does not understand a new value may fail, which results in either loss of connectivity if it declines to forward the traffic, or loss of security if it forwards traffic whose values are part of an attack. Assigning known values for experiments lets such analyzers take a known action for explicitly experimental traffic.

The experimental IPv4 options defined in Section 2.5 are not included in the IPsec Authentication Header calculations, so their use cannot be authenticated. Users of the experimental IPv6 options defined in Section 3.5 can choose whether the option is included in those calculations by choosing the value of the chg field.

Finally, within an administratively self-contained network domain, the administrators should ensure that each code point is used consistently, to avoid interference between experiments. When experimental code points cross several administrative domains, experimenters should assume that other experiments may be using the same code points at the same time, and pay attention to the security threats that such interference might create.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls and other security tools may not know what an experimental value means, and may block the traffic or let it through unchecked. The RFC also warns that two experiments elsewhere could pick the same numbers by accident.
